text:
This source frames farm biosecurity as a set of practical, low-cost, no-special-skill-required daily habits - the main requirement is discipline in following them consistently - organized around three areas: isolation, monitoring/access control, and hygiene.

1. Isolation - protecting your flock from outside sources:
- Any newly acquired poultry should be kept isolated from the existing flock for at least 14 days before mixing them, to confirm the new birds are healthy; this period can be shortened to about 2 weeks if the farm already has a secure boundary fence.
- Know where new poultry actually come from, and avoid buying from unclear or mixed sources, or from middlemen who collect birds from many different farms and mix them together - this is flagged as a major disease-introduction risk.
- Consider vaccinating against diseases common in the local area (e.g. Newcastle disease).
- Manage drinking water sources carefully: avoid ponds or waterways frequented by wild or migratory birds, which can carry the virus.
- Keep ducks/geese separate from chickens or other poultry raised for eggs/meat, including separate feeding and watering areas, since mixing increases exposure risk.
- If disease is suspected in your flock or in the surrounding area, take samples (e.g. from feces or dead birds) for testing.
- If a neighboring farm has a suspected outbreak, do not let people or animals move into or out of your own farm, and report the situation to the relevant authority immediately.
- Keep the coop/enclosure properly fenced and locked, with equipment dedicated solely to your own flock (not shared with other farms).
- Limit visitors; if visitors must enter, they should not wear their own outdoor footwear or clothing into the coop area - consider providing dedicated footwear for visitors to use on-site.

2. Monitoring and access control - both inside and outside the farm:
- Fence the poultry area, since outside animals (including other people's animals) can pose a disease risk to your flock.
- Assess how much risk you're willing to accept from predators or other animals that could enter the coop area.
- Prevent wild animals and rats from accessing feed storage.
- Watch for stray cats and dogs, and ask neighbors to keep their pets away from your poultry area.

3. Hygiene - cleanliness of people, equipment, and housing:
- Wash hands with soap and water after handling poultry or poultry products; this source notes handwashing with soap can substantially reduce (illustratively, roughly 50-55%) the amount of pathogen carried on hands, though exact reduction will vary by situation.
- Clean housing and the surrounding area regularly (sweeping, clearing bedding/litter).
- Clean before disinfecting: physically remove dirt and debris first, then wash, before applying disinfectant - disinfectant applied over visible dirt is not effective. Clean and disinfect all equipment used (feeders, shovels, etc.); this source mentions products like TH4 or lime can be used to disinfect soil and coop surfaces.
- Bury dead birds and any contaminated poultry products at least about 1 meter deep, covering the burial site well afterward so scavenging animals cannot dig them up.
- Remove clutter (food scraps, bottles, cans, containers) from the poultry area promptly, since it can attract rats, insects, and other pests that help spread disease.

If you suspect illness in your flock, consult with a trusted contact (e.g. a village animal health worker) promptly - catching and reporting a problem early gives the best chance of controlling it before it spreads further.
